statement.title: European Central Bank monetary policy statement, 30 April 2026
European Central Bank monetary policy statement, 10 September 2026
paragraphs: The Governing Council today decided to raise the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period. Today’s decision underscores the Governing Council’s commitment to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at its 2% target in the medium term.

The baseline of the new ECB staff projections sees headline inflation averaging 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028. For inflation excluding energy and food, the baseline foresees 2.5% in 2026, 2.6% in 2027 and 2.3% in 2028. Compared with June, the baseline projection for inflation in 2026 is unchanged, while it has been revised up for 2027 and 2028. The baseline projection for economic growth is 0.9% for 2026, 1.4% for 2027 and 1.5% for 2028. This is an upward revision for both 2026 and 2027, mainly reflecting the greater than expected resilience of the euro area economy.

The outlook remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside for inflation and to the downside for economic growth. In relation to the energy shock, the updated scenarios put together by staff illustrate the broad range of outcomes for how growth and inflation would evolve under different assumptions about its intensity and duration, as well as its indirect and second-round effects.

With today’s decision, the Governing Council remains well positioned to navigate the uncertainty caused by the conflict. It will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. In particular, the Governing Council’s interest rate decisions will be based on its assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. The Governing Council is not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

The Governing Council decided to raise the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points. Accordingly, the interest rates on the deposit facility, the main refinancing operations and the marginal lending facility will be increased to 2.50%, 2.65% and 2.90% respectively, with effect from 16 September 2026.
Asset purchase programme (APP) and pandemic emergency purchase programme (PEPP)
The APP and PEPP portfolios are declining at a measured and predictable pace, as the Eurosystem no longer reinvests the principal payments from maturing securities.

The Governing Council stands ready to adjust all of its instruments within its mandate to ensure that inflation stabilises at its 2% target in the medium term and to preserve the smooth functioning of monetary policy transmission. Moreover, the Transmission Protection Instrument is available to counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that pose a serious threat to the transmission of monetary policy across all euro area countries, thus allowing the Governing Council to more effectively deliver on its price stability mandate.
The President of the ECB will comment on the considerations underlying these decisions at a press conference starting at 14:45 CET today.

EUR:account:2026-09-10.label: Account
EUR:account:2026-09-10.title: Meeting of 9-10 September 2026
points: Members assessed that the euro area economy had proved resilient in the second quarter, and the staff growth projections were revised up for 2026 and 2027.
Members judged underlying inflation to have remained contained so far, while core inflation edged down to 2.4% in August from 2.5% in July.
Members assessed that monetary policy transmission had been smooth, and that higher interest rates would support inflation’s return to around target towards the end of 2027.
All members supported raising the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points.
Members reiterated that future interest rate decisions would be data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting, without pre-committing to a particular rate path.

Although all measures continued to stand above 2%, underlying inflation was judged to have remained contained so far.

EUR:speech:4aa2eb3e52ea.label: Speech
EUR:speech:4aa2eb3e52ea.title: Frank Elderson: Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity
points: Member of the Executive Board Frank Elderson says nature provides services without which large parts of economies could not function, and 72% of companies in the euro area depend on at least one ecosystem service.

Member of the Executive Board Frank Elderson says depleted natural capital is disrupting production, damaging supply chains and increasing costs, with consequences spreading into the financial system.

Member of the Executive Board Frank Elderson says research found a 1-in-100-year drought event could put up to 24% of euro area economic output at risk, while nearly 12% faces risks from insufficient flood protection.

Member of the Executive Board Frank Elderson says economic security depends on ecological security and investment in nature is investment in the productive capacity that makes lasting prosperity possible.

Member of the Executive Board Frank Elderson says nature-related risks are increasingly part of ECB work, and the ECB expects banks to identify and manage not only material climate risks, but also nature-related risks.

Member of the Executive Board Frank Elderson says protecting and restoring natural infrastructure will require substantially greater private capital flows towards nature-positive investments alongside public finance, and delay makes restoration more costly and difficult.

fragments.text: Nature provides services without which large parts of our economies could not function.
Our own analysis shows that 72% of companies in the euro area depend on at least one ecosystem service.
Depleted natural capital is already disrupting production, damaging supply chains and increasing costs.
The consequences are already spreading from ecosystems to firms, from firms to balance sheets and from balance sheets into the financial system.
Research involving the ECB, the London School of Economics and Oxford University has found that a 1-in-100-year drought event could put up to 24% of euro area economic output at risk.[5]
Nearly 12% of economic output in the euro area faces risks from insufficient flood protection.[6]
Economic security depends on ecological security.
It is investment in the productive capacity that makes lasting prosperity possible.
Because nature degradation can affect price stability, financial stability and the safety and soundness of banks, nature-related risks are increasingly part of the bread and butter of our work.
In banking supervision, we expect banks to identify and manage not only material climate risks, but also nature-related risks, as part of ensuring banks remain safe and sound.[13]

Protecting and restoring the natural infrastructure on which economic activity depends will require mobilising substantially greater private capital flows towards nature-positive investments, alongside public finance.[17]
But the longer we delay restoring natural capital, the more costly and difficult restoration becomes.

EUR:speech:517b42d1a3c0.title: Philip R. Lane: Diagnostic Challenges for ECB Monetary Policy
points: Member of the Executive Board Philip R. Lane says ECB interest rate decisions are based on the inflation outlook and its risks, underlying inflation, and the strength of monetary policy transmission.

Member of the Executive Board Philip R. Lane says the September inflation data show headline inflation at 3.8 per cent, while underlying inflation indicators show no upward shift in medium-term inflation has taken hold.

Member of the Executive Board Philip R. Lane says fiscal policy, AI and financial conditions are shaping euro area output and inflation dynamics, requiring a multi-pronged diagnostic assessment.

Member of the Executive Board Philip R. Lane says it was prudent to raise the policy rate from 2.00 to 2.50 per cent in June and September, and future decisions will be meeting-by-meeting and data-dependent.

quotes.text: Our interest rate decisions are based on three criteria: (i) our assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data; (ii) the dynamics of underlying inflation; and (iii) the strength of monetary policy transmission.
With non-energy inflation remaining contained so far, underlying inflation indicators indicate that an upward shift in medium-term inflation has not taken hold.
However, our September projections do anticipate an increase in non-energy inflation from 2.3 per cent in 2026 to an average of 2.6 per cent in 2027 before falling back to 2.3 per cent in 2028.[10]
This means that the appropriate monetary policy should not be interpreted as solely driven by the energy supply shock but rather requires a multi-pronged diagnostic assessment.
However, we are not on a pre-committed rate path.

EUR:speech:9e3a13c4decf.label: Speech
EUR:speech:9e3a13c4decf.title: Isabel Schnabel: Monetary policy in a world of overlapping shocks
points: Member of the Executive Board Isabel Schnabel says that since June the Governing Council has raised the key ECB interest rates by 50 basis points, lifting the deposit facility rate from 2% to 2.5%.
Member of the Executive Board Isabel Schnabel says that the effect of a shock on the projected path of inflation, rather than whether it is demand or supply, matters for the optimal policy response.

Member of the Executive Board Isabel Schnabel says that the ECB’s recent policy decisions respond to overlapping shocks, and ECB staff assess their size, persistence, transmission and implications for inflation and economic activity.

Member of the Executive Board Isabel Schnabel says that the ECB complements the baseline with scenario analysis and places greater emphasis on measures of underlying inflation in its communication and analysis.

Member of the Executive Board Isabel Schnabel says that September staff projections foresee HICP inflation dropping from 3.0% this year to 2.1% in 2028, while HICP inflation excluding energy and food is expected to rise to 2.6% in 2027 before falling to 2.3% in 2028.

fragments.text: Since June, the Governing Council has raised the key ECB interest rates by 50 basis points, lifting the deposit facility rate from 2% to 2.5%
the distinction between supply and demand shocks does not alter the direction of the optimal policy response.

EUR:speech:c66aeb50a0f6.label: Speech
EUR:speech:c66aeb50a0f6.title: Philip R. Lane: Euro liquidity lines and the international monetary system
points: Member of the Executive Board Philip R. Lane says the ECB injects liquidity through refinancing operations and asset portfolios, while international liquidity lines complement its domestic liquidity framework.

Member of the Executive Board Philip R. Lane says international liquidity lines are designed to be drawn down only in response to shocks and in crisis situations, while their existence can help to prevent adverse market dynamics.

Member of the Executive Board Philip R. Lane says the ECB decided this year to enhance EUREP, with standing access in principle for all central banks, and onboarded central banks will be able to draw from the facility as of the fourth quarter of 2026.

Member of the Executive Board Philip R. Lane says EUREP loans are priced at the main refinancing operations rate plus a Governing Council spread, have maturities from one day to one week, and have a maximum line size of €50 billion per central bank.

Member of the Executive Board Philip R. Lane says swap lines complement EUREP, can be deployed against local-currency collateral, and should be provided only to foreign central banks clearly capable of repaying their euro debt in due course.

Member of the Executive Board Philip R. Lane says liquidity lines can boost the international role of the euro and support expanded issuance of euro-denominated debt, while greater international use of the euro supports the ECB’s ability to achieve price stability.

EUR:speech:e545c030814a.title: Christine Lagarde: IMFC Statement
points: President Lagarde says the global economy has proven surprisingly resilient, while risks remain tilted to the downside for growth and to the upside for inflation.
President Lagarde says the September ECB staff projections foresee growth of 0.9% in 2026, 1.4% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028.
President Lagarde says headline inflation increased to 3.8% in September, and higher energy prices are expected to keep headline inflation well above target into the first half of 2027.
President Lagarde says the Governing Council decided to raise the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points in September, and that a measured response remains appropriate to keep inflation in check.

President Lagarde says sources of risk and vulnerabilities for euro area financial stability remain high, while private credit in isolation is unlikely to be a source of financial instability in the euro area.
President Lagarde says the Eurosystem is preparing to complement cash with the digital euro and will run a 12-month internal pilot in the second half of 2027.

In relation to the energy shock, the updated scenarios put together by staff illustrate the broad range of outcomes for how growth and inflation would evolve under different assumptions about its intensity and duration, as well as its indirect and second-round effects.

quotes.text: The Governing Council today decided to raise the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points.
The baseline projection for economic growth is 0.9% for 2026, 1.4% for 2027 and 1.5% for 2028.
The Governing Council is not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

Accordingly, the interest rates on the deposit facility, the main refinancing operations and the marginal lending facility will be increased to 2.50%, 2.65% and 2.90% respectively, with effect from 16 September 2026.
The APP and PEPP portfolios are declining at a measured and predictable pace, as the Eurosystem no longer reinvests the principal payments from maturing securities.

EXACT.label: EXACT
EXACT.help: Solved exactly from 1M month-average futures: the rate changes only on the effective date, so the implied rate after the meeting follows from the monthly average.

CURVE.label: CURVE
CURVE.help: OIS curve: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY and CHF use the Eurex Clearing settlement curves (discount factors), with the overnight rate fitted as constant between effective dates (one rate per interval); elsewhere an OIS forward curve averaged over the interval. Minus the overnight-to-policy spread.

ESTIMATE.label: ESTIMATE
ESTIMATE.help: No contract isolates this meeting: 1M/3M futures averages fitted with the rate changing only on effective dates and the smallest possible step changes. NZD also uses an estimated BKBM-OCR spread.

UPPER_BOUND.label: UPPER BOUND
UPPER_BOUND.help: 3M contract window: the average covers several meetings, so the cumulative move is an upper bound for this meeting alone.

PROXY.label: PROXY
PROXY.help: Government-curve proxy - not policy-equivalent. Shown as a raw sovereign level unless a basis can be measured from a short tenor.

DECIDED.label: DECIDED
DECIDED.help: The meeting has already been decided: it is part of the base rate.

level_help.bkbm: BKBM base: level of the ASX 90-day bank bill, not the OCR - no BKBM-OCR spread exists, so no bp vs the OCR
level_help.sovereign_proxy: sovereign proxy: raw government-curve level, not policy-equivalent

methodology.title: Base rate
methodology.text: The last rate DECIDED on or before the as-of date, including a decision that has been announced but is not in force yet (shown as 'from <date>'). The Fed is the midpoint of the target range.

methodology.title: Implied policy rate
methodology.text: Market instruments give the overnight benchmark path; the benchmark-to-policy spread (median of the last 20 business days, excluding +-2 business days around rate changes and month-ends) is removed to get a policy-equivalent rate.

methodology.title: Methods
methodology.text: EXACT: 1M month-average futures chain. CURVE: OIS curve - for USD (fed funds), EUR (EUR STR), GBP (SONIA), JPY (TONA) and CHF (SARON) the daily Eurex Clearing settlement curves: the overnight rate is taken as constant between effective dates and fitted to the published discount factors (least squares, one rate per interval, a small smoothing term only where pillars cannot separate two intervals), then the overnight-to-policy spread is removed (EFFR vs the Fed midpoint, EUR STR vs the deposit rate, SONIA vs Bank Rate, the call rate vs the BoJ guideline, SARON vs the SNB rate); a meeting whose effective date is beyond the last pillar is n/a. Otherwise an OIS forward curve averaged between effective dates. UPPER BOUND: 3M contracts whose window spans several meetings. PROXY: government curves / bills, with a basis measured only from tenors observed before the first effective date - without one ('proxy without short end') no bp, step or probability is computed and only the raw level is shown.

methodology.title: Estimates (ESTIMATE)
methodology.text: Where no contract isolates a meeting (CAD beyond the 1M CORRA chain, NZD bank bills), every 1M / 3M futures contract of the exchange is fitted at once: the overnight rate is constant between effective dates, each contract's average over its window equals 100 minus its price (days already past use the realised fixings), and among the paths that fit, the one with the smallest step changes is chosen. The step of an estimated meeting is its level minus the level of the previous point; a meeting no contract reaches is n/a and its move is inside the next one. No probability is computed for an estimate. NZD: bank bills are a BKBM level; the BKBM-OCR spread is an estimate (median of 3M interbank minus OCR over months without an OCR change around them), not a daily observation. If the actual BKBM-OCR spread is wider than assumed, every NZD point is lower by about the same number of bp.

methodology.title: Step and probability
methodology.text: For EXACT and CURVE the implied step at the next meeting is split into whole 25 bp moves (n = floor(|step|/25)) and a fraction p of one more: P(n+1 moves) = p, P(n moves) = 1 - p, in the direction of the step.

methodology.title: Cumulative bp
methodology.text: Implied policy rate after the last meeting of the year minus the base rate, in bp. Positive = hawkish.

methodology.title: Repricing
methodology.text: Change of the implied level at a fixed horizon (last meeting of 2026 / 2027) over 5 business days (1w) and 21 business days (1m); independent of decisions taken in between. The change of the cumulative bp is a secondary field.

methodology.title: GAP
methodology.text: Market minus bank, in bp: the Fed's median dot vs the implied rate at the last meeting of each year. Only where both are on the same basis.

methodology.title: Surprises and reaction
methodology.text: Surprise vs consensus: decided rate minus consensus. Surprise vs market: decided step minus the step implied at T-1 (EXACT / CURVE / PROXY with a basis only). Reaction: change of the implied level between the close of T-1 and T at the next meeting and at the last meeting of the year.

methodology.title: Pairs
methodology.text: Base minus quote, metric by metric: the current rate differential (carry), the implied differential at year end (both legs policy-equivalent) and its repricing (both legs need a change of level). The flag is the weaker of the two legs.

latency.title: Time from decision to site
latency.text: First seen = the moment the collector stored the statement; official time = the decision time in the bank's zone (the BoJ announces at a variable time: its own RSS timestamp). Target: within 15 minutes. An external trigger starts the collector at the decision; before it existed the statements were found by the regular runs.
